history.heading: A Swedish chapter
paragraphs: Saint Barthélemy (St. Barts), a small volcanic island in the northeastern Caribbean, was named by Columbus after his brother Bartolomeo. French settlers arrived in 1648. The dry, rocky island was unsuitable for large plantations, and its settlers were mostly small farmers and fishermen from Normandy and Brittany.

In 1784 France ceded the island to Sweden in exchange for trading rights. The capital was renamed Gustavia after King Gustav III, and it became a free port. Sweden sold the island back to France in 1878. Many street names still recall the Swedish period.

history.heading: Becoming a collectivity
paragraphs: The island was part of Guadeloupe until 2007, when it became a separate French overseas collectivity. Hurricane Irma caused severe damage in 2017.

culture.heading: Island identity
paragraphs: French is the official language, and an old Norman dialect is still spoken by some residents. Most of the population is of European descent, unlike most Caribbean islands. Catholicism is the main religion. The island is known for luxury and celebrities, as well as its beaches.

politics.heading: French overseas collectivity
paragraphs: Saint Barthélemy is an overseas collectivity of France with its own territorial council and president, and wide powers over taxes and local matters. It left the European Union's territory in 2012, becoming an associated overseas country and territory.

economy.heading: Luxury tourism
paragraphs: The economy is based on luxury tourism, with high-end villas, yachts and boutiques. There is no income tax for long-term residents. The currency is the euro.
